new_statements.quote: For details of the phonological and lexical subgrouping of these languages, see Bradley (1979a). Basically, all share an innovative two-way tonal contrast in original stop-final syllables; the Northern Loloish languages have mostly reversed phonetic values for these two tones compared to other Loloish languages. Central Loloish is characterised by extensive tonal splits leading to complex tonal systems including contour tones. ... Within this cluster there are also several smaller groups: the Phana of Laos (about 500) and the Sila or Sida of Laos and Vietnam (about 2,000).

tone_statements.quote: Typologically, Pana and Khmu differ markedly. Pana is an subject-object-verb language. Phonologically, the language is tonal, making three basic tonal distinctions. Vowels can be nasalized or feature laryngealization, similar to the ‘creaky tone’ of Burmese. Pana words are generally monosyllabic, and have simple consonant-vowel-tone syllable structure. The history of Pana has been one of an ever simplifying syllable, in which final consonants have been lost and initial clusters reduced. The Khmu spoken in Bopiat, on the other hand, is non-tonal with subject-verb-object word order.

tone.quote: Typologically, Pana and Khmu differ markedly. Pana is an subject-object-verb language. Phonologically, the language is tonal, making three basic tonal distinctions. Vowels can be nasalized or feature laryngealization, similar to the ‘creaky tone’ of Burmese. Pana words are generally monosyllabic, and have simple consonant-vowel-tone syllable structure. The history of Pana has been one of an ever simplifying syllable, in which final consonants have been lost and initial clusters reduced. The Khmu spoken in Bopiat, on the other hand, is non-tonal with subject-verb-object word order.

tone.says: First-hand typological profile: Pana is tonal with three basic tonal distinctions; vowels may be nasalized or laryngealized ('creaky tone' like Burmese); words mostly monosyllabic with CV+tone syllables; finals lost and clusters reduced historically; contrasts it with non-tonal Khmu of the same village. No tone values or minimal sets given (sociolinguistic article).
